discoveries.explanation: Best guess: two stars eclipsing each other (an eclipsing binary). A dip of 9.448% repeats every 3.7842 days and lasts about 1.6 hours. There is a second, shallower dip at phase 0.46 (6.382% deep, 68% of the main dip). A dip that big halfway round the orbit means the companion gives off a lot of light itself, like a star does. This matches TIC 231010756 (TESS EB catalogue) on the TESS Eclipsing Binary catalogue (Prsa et al. 2022) (same period).

vetting.reason: The dip stands 2780 times above the noise over 12 events.

vetting.name: odd_even
vetting.reason: Alternate dips have matching depths (9.389% vs 9.500%), as expected for a planet.

vetting.name: secondary_eclipse
vetting.reason: There is a second, shallower dip at phase 0.46 (6.382% deep, 68% of the main dip). A dip that big halfway round the orbit means the companion gives off a lot of light itself, like a star does.

vetting.name: size
vetting.reason: Dip depth 9.448% on a 0.98 R_sun star implies about 2.93 Jupiter radii (32.9 Earth radii), likely range 2.76-3.10. Even the low end is bigger than any known planet (limit 2 Jupiter radii), so it is too large to be a planet.
